name: Binary Subsequence Rotation
description: Naman has two binary strings $$$s$$$ and $$$t$$$ of length $$$n$$$ (a binary string is a string which only consists of the characters " 0 " and " 1 "). He wants to convert $$$s$$$ into $$$t$$$ using the following operation as few times as possible. In one operation, he can choose any subsequence of $$$s$$$ and rotate it clockwise once. For example, if $$$s = 1\textbf{1}101\textbf{00}$$$, he can choose a subsequence corresponding to indices ($$$1$$$-based) $$$\{2, 6, 7 \}$$$ and rotate them clockwise. The resulting string would then be $$$s = 1\textbf{0}101\textbf{10}$$$. A string $$$a$$$ is said to be a subsequence of string $$$b$$$ if $$$a$$$ can be obtained from $$$b$$$ by deleting some characters without changing the ordering of the remaining characters. To perform a clockwise rotation on a sequence $$$c$$$ of size $$$k$$$ is to perform an operation which sets $$$c_1:=c_k, c_2:=c_1, c_3:=c_2, \ldots, c_k:=c_{k-1}$$$ simultaneously. Determine the minimum number of operations Naman has to perform to convert $$$s$$$ into $$$t$$$ or say that it is impossible.
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer $$$n$$$ $$$(1 \le n \le 10^6)$$$ — the length of the strings. The second line contains the binary string $$$s$$$ of length $$$n$$$. The third line contains the binary string $$$t$$$ of length $$$n$$$.
output_specification: If it is impossible to convert $$$s$$$ to $$$t$$$ after any number of operations, print $$$-1$$$. Otherwise, print the minimum number of operations required.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1370E — Binary Subsequence Rotation [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
